newsitem.title: THAILAND: Deadlock over new Thai PM prompts calls for polls.
newsitem.headline: Deadlock over new Thai PM prompts calls for polls.

text.p: The deadlock faced by Thailand's six-party ruling coalition in finding a successor to premier Banharn Silpa-archa prompted calls by the business community on Friday for a general election.

Analysts and private polls gave a cool response to the prospect of Defence Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh replacing Banharn, who was pressured last Saturday by his allies to declare his resignation within seven days.
They said any new government led by the former army chief would be unlikely to introduce initiatives to change partisan Thai politics or revive public confidence amid a slowing national economy.

A Thai Farmers Research Centre poll said 42.3 percent of 410 students, civil servants and businessmen questioned this week favoured fresh elections, while 40.9 favoured the current coalition. The rest had no firm opinion.

"With Chavalit at the helm, leading the same coalition, we would basically have the old team doing things the way it has been doing them in the past 14 months. I don't see any improvement," said a market analyst who declined to be named.
He said a Chavalit-led government might not last long as it would lack popular support and likely be weakened by political infighting.

Banharn's core Chart Thai Party, with 91 seats, is divided on its support for Chavalit. Coalition sources said Banharn was not in favour of Chavalit succeeding him because he believed the defence minister had engineered his downfall.

Banharn told Chart Thai members early this week that he had been blackmailed by Chavalit last Saturday into announcing his resignation plan in return for coalition support to help him win a no-confidence vote in parliament.
Chart Thai's popularity among urban Thais has suffered a heavy setback in the past year and it lacks a strong party candidate to challenge Chavalit for the top job.
Some 49.8 percent of those questioned in the Thai Farmers poll said the current coalition would fail to restore political stability.
Somjai Phagaphasvivat, a political lecturer at Thammasat University, and other economists said Banharn should call a snap election even if it meant breaking his pledge to resign.

Analysts said current political uncertainty, and the several weeks time that a new prime minister would need to form his cabinet, would leave an administrative vacuum that could disrupt government efforts to shore up the economy.

Thai exports rose a meagre 2.9 percent during January-July against 26.5 percent a year ago. Private economists expected Thailand's 1996 gross domestic product to grow at its slowest pace in a decade -- about seven percent against 8.6 in 1995.
"We've given up hopes on the economy picking up in the last quarter as everybody will be occupied with politics in the next two months," said Porametr Suwansiri of Bangkok Nomura Securities Plc.
"Exports and corporate earnings look gloomy. We're now trying to see ahead for any signs of recovery in 1997," he said.
Analysts said Chavalit's only asset was his ally Amnuay Viravan, leader of Nam Thai Party, who would likely lead a new economic team under any Chavalit administration.
But the Thai Farmers poll said 48.2 percent of people questioned picked Amnuay, current foreign and deputy prime minister, as the most suitable candidate to replace Banharn.
